opus-5.5.text:
I think there's real truth to it, but "simply" is doing a lot of work in that sentence.

Test-time compute is a genuinely new axis, and it's been an important unlock. For a long time we had one knob: make the model bigger, train it on more data, spend more on pre-training. Then we realized that letting the model think, reason through a problem, try something, check its work, and backtrack makes a huge difference on hard tasks like math, code, and multi-step planning. Those were exactly the areas where models were weakest. So it's not a gimmick. It's a real capability gain.

But I'm skeptical of the framing that it's just another scaling curve we ride up until we get everything we need. A few reasons.

First, it isn't free. When you scale pre-training, you pay once and amortize the cost across every query. When you scale test-time compute, you pay on every single query. For enterprises running millions of calls a day, that changes the economics a lot. A model that's slightly smarter but ten times more expensive and much slower is the wrong tool for most production workloads. So the question becomes how efficiently you reason, not just how much.

Second, reasoning works best where you can verify the answer: math, code, things with a clear right answer and a clean feedback signal. Much of what businesses actually need is messier: drafting, judgment calls, navigating ambiguous internal data. Thinking longer helps there too, but the gains are less dramatic and harder to measure.

Third, and this is the big one for me, I don't think the bottleneck for most real-world value is raw intelligence anymore. It's integration. Can the model access the right data? Can it use the tools inside a company's systems? Is it secure, private, deployable where the customer needs it? You can give a model all the thinking time in the world, but if it can't see your CRM or your codebase, it can't do the job. Scaling test-time compute doesn't solve that.

So I see it as one important ingredient. It's a great new lever, and we use it. But the idea that we just turn this dial and capabilities fall out is too simple. The next phase is going to be much more about efficiency, data, tool use, and actually fitting these systems into how people work.

r002.rationale: It challenges the idea that test-time compute is a straightforward scaling curve, describes it as a new axis involving reasoning, and says simply turning the dial is too simplistic.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's half right, and the half that's wrong matters a lot.

The part that's right is that test-time compute is clearly a real lever. If you let a model think longer, search over more candidate answers, verify its own work, you get better outputs. We saw that with chain of thought years ago, and the reasoning models have made it much more systematic. So in that narrow sense, yes, it's another axis you can scale, and the curves look reasonably clean.

Where I push back is the word "simply." Pretraining scale and inference scale are not interchangeable. Pretraining gives you knowledge and priors, the raw material. Test-time compute lets you spend more effort combining what's already there. If the model fundamentally doesn't know something, or has a broken world model about some domain, no amount of thinking longer fixes that. You're just searching more thoroughly over a space that doesn't contain the answer.

The other thing people underweight is the economics. Pretraining is a cost you pay once and amortize across every query forever. Test-time compute is a cost you pay every single time someone asks a question. So when a lab says, "Look, we hit this benchmark by letting the model think for ten minutes," that's a scientific result, but it's not a product result. For most enterprise workloads, nobody is going to wait ten minutes or pay a hundred times the inference bill for a marginal improvement. The question I actually care about is: what's the capability you get at a fixed, reasonable cost per query? And on that axis, a lot of the headline gains shrink considerably.

So my view is that it's a genuine, important tool, and it's been underexplored relative to pretraining, so there's low-hanging fruit. But treating it as the thing that gets us all the way there is, I think, a bit of a narrative that's convenient for the moment. It fills the gap while pretraining gains are slowing, and it's much more compute-flattering in the short term. The capabilities that actually matter, the ones that let a model do a multi-week task reliably in a real company, still come from a combination of better data, better training, and better tooling around the model. Thinking longer helps. It's not the whole story.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s another important axis of scaling, but I’m skeptical of the word “simply.” With training, you spend compute up front and then amortize that investment across everyone who uses the model. With test-time compute, you’re paying for that extra work every time you answer a question. So the economics are quite different.

The exciting part is that you don’t necessarily need an immediate answer to every problem. If you’re asking a system to solve a difficult research question, you might happily wait a while if that produces a much better result. But for a lot of everyday interactions, speed and cost matter enormously.

So I think the question is: can the model use that additional compute productively? Can it explore alternatives, check its work, and recognize when it’s going down the wrong path? Just making it generate more tokens doesn’t guarantee that. It’s a promising direction, but I wouldn’t take the existence of another scaling axis as proof that it delivers every capability we need.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s something real there, but I’d be cautious about the word “simply.” At training time, you’re spending compute to build a model that can solve a broad range of problems. At test time, you’re giving that model more opportunity to work on a particular problem—to explore alternatives, check its work, and revise an answer.

That’s powerful when you have a way to tell whether you’re making progress. With code, for example, you can run tests. But for a lot of tasks, evaluating the answer is itself difficult. More thinking doesn’t automatically mean better thinking; you need a process that makes productive use of that extra compute.

So I see it as another important axis of scaling. I don’t think we can jump from that to saying it will produce every capability we need. The interesting question is which problems improve with more computation at inference, how reliably they improve, and whether the improvement is worth the cost and latency.
